title: Object-Oriented Python
objectives: Define a class with __init__, instance attributes and methods, and construct instances of it
Control output with __str__ and enforce invariants by validating attributes in __init__
Create subclasses that extend __init__ with super() and override inherited methods
Explain the difference between class attributes (shared) and instance attributes (per-object), and avoid the shared mutable attribute bug
motivation: A position is more than three numbers in a dict - it carries rules: quantities are positive, market value depends on a live price, PnL is measured against average cost. Dicts enforce nothing; a typo like position['qtyy'] silently creates a new key. A class bundles the data with the code that guards and uses it, so invalid states become impossible instead of inevitable. Every framework you will meet - pandas Series, order objects in a trading API - is classes all the way down.

blocks.md: A **class** is a blueprint; an **instance** is one object built from it. The __init__ method runs automatically at construction and stores attributes on `self` - the instance being built. Every method takes `self` as its first parameter, and Python passes the instance automatically: pos.market_value(42.25) means 'call market_value with self = pos'. The convention is a single leading pattern: classes in CamelCase, attributes and methods in snake_case.

blocks.caption: __init__ stores three attributes; market_value and pnl read them through self; __str__ decides what print shows.

blocks.md: Methods with double underscores like __init__ and __str__ are called **dunder** methods - hooks Python calls for you: construction calls __init__, print() calls __str__. Defining __str__ turns debugging dumps from `<__main__.Position object at 0x...>` into one readable line, which matters once a portfolio holds a thousand of these objects.

The dict version of a position works - until it does not. Dicts accept any typo as a new key, nothing stops a negative quantity, and the PnL formula lives wherever it was copy-pasted. A class fixes all three at once: attributes are checked by name at development time, __init__ can validate, and every rule lives in exactly one method.

blocks.caption: Run the block and read the traceback: the invalid position now fails at construction, not three days later in a report.

blocks.md: A subclass extends a parent class: write `class HedgedPosition(Position):` and it starts with everything Position has. Override a method by redefining it, and call super() to reach the parent's version - the standard pattern inside __init__ so the parent's set-up runs before the child's additions. Use inheritance for genuine is-a relationships and keep hierarchies shallow; deep trees are harder to read than a few well-placed methods.

blocks.caption: The subclass reuses the parent's __init__ via super(), then overrides market_value.

blocks.title: Class attributes are shared by every instance
blocks.md: An attribute assigned at class level (outside __init__) lives on the class, so all instances see the same value. That is correct for constants - and a bug factory when the value is a mutable list. Always initialise per-object state with self.x = ... inside __init__.

blocks.code:
class Portfolio:
    positions = []            # ONE list shared by every instance!

p1 = Portfolio()
p2 = Portfolio()
p1.positions.append('AAPL')
print(p2.positions)           # ['AAPL'] - p2 sees p1's edit
blocks.caption: The fix: define __init__ and set self.positions = [] there, giving each instance its own list.
Instance attributes live in the object's __dict__ - a hash table like the dicts of lesson py-collections - which is why attribute access is an O(1) average lookup.

blocks.md: You now write objects that own their data and their rules, extend them cleanly, and know the shared-attribute trap that bites most newcomers. The final lesson in this module adds the tools that make Python code elegant at scale: iterators, generators, decorators and context managers.

guidedExercise.prompt: Build a `Portfolio` class that starts empty, has an `add(symbol, qty, avg_cost)` method storing each position in an internal dict keyed by symbol (each value a dict of qty and avg_cost), and a `market_value(prices)` method taking a symbol-to-price dict and returning the sum of qty x price over all positions. Add AAPL (250 @ 41.75) and MSFT (100 @ 43.00), then value it against prices AAPL 42.25 and MSFT 43.50.
hints: Set self.positions = {} inside __init__ - never as a class attribute.
Iterate self.positions.items() to get symbol and position dict together.

independentExercise.prompt: Extend the Portfolio class from the guided exercise with (1) a `pnl(prices)` method returning the total PnL across positions using each stored avg_cost, and (2) a `__str__` method returning 'Portfolio with N positions'. Then construct the same book (AAPL 250 @ 41.75, MSFT 100 @ 43.00), print its PnL against prices AAPL 42.25 / MSFT 43.50, and print the portfolio itself.
hints: PnL per position is (price - avg_cost) * qty; sum them with the same loop shape as market_value.
len(self.positions) is the position count for __str__.

commonMistakes: Forgetting self as the first parameter of every method, or calling it something else - pos.market_value(p) passes pos automatically.
Assigning a mutable class attribute (positions = [] at class level) so all instances share one list; initialise per-object state in __init__.
Repeating the parent's set-up in a subclass instead of calling super().__init__(...).
Leaving out __str__, so debugging prints <__main__.Position object at 0x...> instead of a readable line.
realWorldApplication: Web frameworks, database clients and every data-science library expose classes: you construct objects, call their methods, and rely on their invariants - so being fluent on both the using and the writing side is a daily skill.
quantFinanceApplication: Position, Order and Portfolio are the canonical domain objects of trading systems: a Portfolio class that validates quantities and computes market value and PnL from a price map is a production pattern in miniature.
summary: A class bundles data and behaviour: __init__ stores attributes on self, methods take self first, and print() calls __str__.
Classes beat plain dicts for records because they validate in __init__ (raise ValueError on bad input) and keep each rule in one method.
Subclasses extend parents with super().__init__(...) and override methods; keep hierarchies shallow.
Class-level attributes are shared by all instances - per-object state must be set as self.x inside __init__, especially mutable containers.

quiz.explanation: __init__ stores the attributes at construction; p.symbol reads one back, and doubled() multiplies self.qty by 2.
Child overrides label() but calls super().label(), which runs the parent's version; the strings concatenate to child-base.
str(t) calls __str__ explicitly, and print(t) calls it implicitly - both show the string __str__ returns.

quiz.prompt: In a method body, what is `self`?
options: The module the class is defined in
The instance the method was called on
quiz.explanation: Python passes the instance automatically: pos.market_value(p) calls market_value with self = pos. self is a convention, not a keyword, but you should never break it.

quiz.prompt: Given `class Portfolio: positions = []` with instances p1 and p2, what happens after `p1.positions.append('AAPL')`?
options: Python copies the list for p2
quiz.explanation: positions is a class attribute, so both instances share one list; the append through p1 is visible through p2. Initialise self.positions = [] in __init__ instead.

quiz.prompt: What is the role of __init__ in a class?
options: It destroys instances when they are deleted
It initialises the instance's attributes when the class is called with Position(...)
It converts the object to a string for printing
It imports the class into other modules
quiz.explanation: __init__ runs automatically at construction and sets up the instance's attributes; __str__ handles printing, and ordinary garbage collection handles teardown.

flashcards.front: What is self in a Python method?
flashcards.back: The instance the method was called on, passed automatically: pos.market_value(p) runs market_value with self = pos. It is a naming convention, not a keyword.

flashcards.front: What does print(pos) show when __str__ is defined?
flashcards.back: Exactly the string __str__ returns - print() calls str(obj), which uses __str__ (falling back to __repr__ if it is absent).
Attributes set at class level are shared by all instances; attributes set as self.x inside __init__ belong to one object. Never make the shared one mutable.
Returns the parent-class view: super().__init__(...) runs the parent's initialiser inside the child's, so subclasses extend rather than duplicate set-up. Methods can be overridden by redefining them.

flashcards.front: class Portfolio: positions = [] - what is the bug?
flashcards.back: positions is a class attribute, so every instance shares ONE list; appends via one instance appear in all. Initialise self.positions = [] inside __init__.
